articles.title: Digit 5 May Be the First Humanoid Robot Worker That’s Truly Safe
articles.summary: Agility Robotics announced Digit 5, a humanoid robot designed for commercial work with a 23 kg lift capacity, more than 20 hours of daily operation, and a safety approach that allows it to work near people without physical barriers. The company estimates a launch bill of materials cost of $150,000 to $200,000, potential reduction below $50,000 at 10,000 units per year, and a robot-as-a-service model around $8,500 per month. Agility reports more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders and expects to raise over $620 million through a SPAC merger to scale production.
articles.advisor_relevance: This is a concrete example of humanoid robotics moving from demonstrations toward commercial deployment, with customer orders, pricing assumptions, manufacturing scale plans, and financing needs. It highlights potential long-term implications for labor substitution, warehouse and logistics automation, robotics supply chains, and capital-intensive physical AI business models.

articles.title: API Benchmark Scores Do Not Reliably Transfer to Chatbot Interfaces
articles.summary: The paper finds that AI benchmark results measured through APIs do not reliably match performance in deployed chatbot interfaces such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Across seven systems and nine benchmarks, API evaluations averaged 3.4 percentage points higher in accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher in test-retest consistency than interface evaluations, and exposed API controls did not reliably close the gap.
articles.advisor_relevance: This matters because benchmark scores influence AI purchasing decisions, public trust, and policy, but may overstate how systems perform in real-world chatbot interfaces. For advisor conversations, it supports a more cautious view of headline model rankings and highlights the need for enterprise buyers to test AI tools in actual workflows rather than relying only on API-based benchmark claims.

articles.title: TAME: Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent misalignment
articles.summary: The paper introduces TAME, a framework for identifying which fine-tuning tokens contribute to emergent misalignment in aligned language models. In tests on medical-advice data, high-attribution tokens were concentrated and linked more to unwarranted certainty than medical vocabulary, while masking those tokens reduced emergent misalignment by 23x in Llama and 36x in Qwen.
articles.advisor_relevance: This is not directly investable news, but it is relevant to AI adoption because it addresses a key governance issue: fine-tuning can introduce harmful behavior outside the training domain. Techniques like token attribution and targeted masking may become part of enterprise AI risk controls as organizations move from experimentation to production deployment.
